messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Professor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mele was a 31-year-old professor, married, who came to treatment months after a life-threatening car crash that she still could not tell in a straight line. She remembered driving home after teaching, the late light flashing across the windshield, and then one piercing instant of absolute clarity: another car suddenly crossing into her lane. After that, her recollection broke apart. There was the violent image of metal folding and glass bursting inward, then nothing she could place, then a sharp fragment of her own hands gripping the wheel, then blankness again. When people asked what happened, including her husband and later colleagues who knew she had been injured, she would begin, get stuck, lose the thread, and stop. Some moments felt burned into her mind with unbearable vividness, while whole stretches were missing, and the disconnected quality of the memory left her feeling as if the worst thing that had happened to her existed in pieces she could neither assemble nor trust.

That broken quality of remembering had started to shape what she believed about herself and her life. Because she could not hold the event together in a coherent account, Mele had come to feel that something essential in her had been damaged. She used to think of herself as engaged, intellectually alive, and at home in the world of her department, her marriage, and her friendships. Now she described herself as always miserable. She felt estranged even in familiar places, as though she no longer belonged anywhere, not fully with her students, not fully with her husband, not even fully inside her own life. The blank spaces in memory made the whole experience feel senseless to her, and from there it was a short step to the conviction that nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore.

Those beliefs fed directly into the way she lived in a state of danger. Because she no longer experienced the world as a place she fit into or could count on, she was certain safety could disappear without warning. At night she would wake abruptly and sit up scanning the bedroom, checking the windows, the hallway, the sounds in the house, needing to confirm that she and her husband were safe. During the day she was continually on guard, especially in parking lots and near traffic, with her attention pulled toward movement, headlights, the angle of passing cars. At times she had sudden episodes in which the crash seemed to be happening again, with a jolt of bodily certainty that made the present moment vanish. The more miserable and unmoored she felt, the more relentlessly she monitored for danger; and living that way only deepened her sense that her old self was gone for good.

Her fragmented memory also seemed to keep the sense of threat alive. Because she could not place the crash into a complete past event, isolated pieces returned as if unfinished. A glimpse of a damaged car on the side of the road, or even a photograph of two vehicles crumpled together in a news story, could pull up one bright shard of impact without context. If someone in the faculty lounge started talking about an accident on the freeway, she would feel her mind slip, unable to stay oriented in the conversation. The lack of a continuous memory made these moments feel less like recollection and more like re-entry into something still underway, which left her more watchful and more convinced that another catastrophe could break through at any moment.

That persistent alertness, in turn, seemed to worsen the way she remembered. When she tried to explain the crash in therapy, or when her husband gently asked what she had gone through, she often became visibly tense, eyes fixed, body rigid, and her account would fragment further under the pressure. The more keyed up she was, the less she could hold onto sequence; she could produce vivid snapshots but not the bridge between them. After nights spent waking repeatedly to check whether she was safe, she would come to campus already strained, and even passing references to accidents or seeing dented cars in the faculty parking lot could bring on a detached, unreal feeling, as if she were no longer fully present in her own body. In those moments, crash-related images and conversations did not register as reminders of something over; they hit her as immediate threats.

Her beliefs also made those triggers more potent. Because she had come to see herself as permanently altered, cut off, and unable to find meaning, any reminder of the collision felt like proof that this ruined version of life was now her real life. A discussion of a student’s commute or a colleague mentioning a highway pileup could make her feel suddenly separate from everyone else in the room, as if they still belonged to an ordinary world and she did not. Even seeing images of wrecked cars could provoke that drifting unreality, followed by a wave of dread and the familiar thought that happiness had ended with the crash. By this point the consequences were showing in her work and marriage: she struggled to stay present during departmental conversations when accidents came up, and at home her husband had stopped asking for details because he could see how quickly she became far away.

What finally brought Mele to seek help was not one single flare-up but the tightening sense that her life was narrowing around the crash. She was frightened by how easily she could be pulled out of the present and by how often she woke in the night to make sure she was safe. Most of all, she feared that the misery and disconnection had become permanent—that she would remain a person with no coherent story of what happened, no real place in her own life, and no way back to meaning. At the same time, she still held a cautious hope that if the crash could somehow become something she remembered rather than something she kept re-entering, she might feel like herself again.
